label: Seasons
rationale: Sets that mark the year in daily talk: blossoms out in spring, summer heat and cicadas, snow lying in winter.
mixUps: semi ga naku uses naku (鳴く, an animal's call), not naku 'cry' (泣く), and pairs with kaminari ga naru: animals naku, things naru. atsusa ni yowai is the osake ga yowai idea with ni (samusa ni yowai for cold), and snow furu as it falls but tsumoru once it lies.

targets.trap: 'The blossoms are out' points to deru, but flowers that are out are saiteru (sakura saiteru); hana ga deru isn't said. Hiraku is the petals opening, mostly in description, not the everyday word. Blossoms coming down are chiru: mou chitchatta (petals already on the ground are ochiteru).
targets.use: Mostly about cherry blossoms in spring: sakura saita? (are they out?), mou saiteru (they're already out), mada saitenai. Saiteru is the flowers being out now, not still opening. Ga is usually dropped.
targets.notes: Peak bloom is mankai (ima mankai da tte), and going to see them is ohanami: ohanami ikanai?

example.ja: ベランダの花、咲いたよ。
example.english: The flowers on the balcony have come out.

examplePolite.romaji: beranda no hana ga sakimashita yo.
examplePolite.ja: ベランダの花が咲きましたよ。
examplePolite.english: The flowers on the balcony have come out.

targets.verbSense: weak, having little strength or tolerance
targets.trap: Atsusa takes ni: atsusa ga yowai isn't said (with osake, ga and ni both work). Atsui no nigate (I can't do heat) is just as everyday.
targets.use: Said about yourself or someone else in summer: atsusa ni yowai n da yo ne (I'm no good in the heat). The cold version, samusa ni yowai, is just as common. The ni stays.
targets.notes: The opposite is atsusa ni tsuyoi; atsusa is atsui + -sa (the heat), like samusa from samui.

example.romaji: atsusa ni yowai n da yo ne.
example.english: I'm no good in the heat.

examplePolite.romaji: atsusa ni yowai n desu yo ne.
examplePolite.ja: 暑さに弱いんですよね。
examplePolite.english: I'm no good in the heat.

targets.verbSense: make its call (an animal, bird or insect)
targets.trap: English has a verb per creature (sing, chirp, buzz, meow), but Japanese uses naku (鳴く) for nearly all of them, and it sounds the same as naku 'cry' (泣く). Tori ga utau is poetic; in talk it's naku.
targets.use: Summer small talk, mostly semi naiteru (the cicadas are going) or semi nakihajimeta ne (the cicadas have started). Casual speech drops ga.
targets.notes: Autumn nights have mushi ga naku (crickets and other insects); a barking dog is usually hoeru.

examplePolite.ja: セミが鳴き始めましたね。

targets.english: snow settles, lies on the ground
targets.trap: English 'the snow's sticking' points to tsuku, but snow building up on the ground is tsumoru; tsuku is snow stuck on things: kuruma ni yuki tsuiteru. Nokotteru is old snow that hasn't melted yet.
targets.use: Mostly as yuki tsumotteru (there's snow on the ground) or tsumoru kana? (will it settle?). Tsumotteru is the snow lying there, while snow still coming down is yuki futteru.
targets.notes: Melting is tokeru: yuki mou toketa ne.

example.ja: 朝起きたら、雪積もってた。
example.english: When I got up, there was snow on the ground.

examplePolite.ja: 朝起きたら、雪が積もってました。
examplePolite.english: When I got up, there was snow on the ground.
